title: "A Brief History of Init Systems"
---

# A Brief History of Init Systems

When the Linux kernel completes initialization, it calls `run_init_process("/sbin/init")`. As **Process ID 1**, this executable is the ancestor of every userspace process on the machine.

Over the past four decades, operating system initialization has evolved across four distinct eras.

```
       Era 1: SysVinit (1980s-2000s)
       - Sequential, shell-script driven, numbered runlevels (0-6)
       - Fragile PID tracking, slow serial execution
                      |
                      v
       Era 2: Event-Driven Prototypes (mid 2000s)
       - Upstart (Ubuntu), Launchd (macOS)
       - Asynchronous event bus, reactive daemon launching
                      |
                      v
       Era 3: The systemd Revolution (2010-Present)
       - Socket activation, cgroup process containment, declarative units
       - Aggressive parallelization, integrated logging (journald)
                      |
                      v
       Era 4: The Minimalist Counter-Movement
       - OpenRC (dependency tree without binary bloat)
       - s6 & runit (composable supervision trees, UNIX philosophy)
```

## Era 1: Classic System V Init (SysVinit)

Originally developed for AT&T UNIX System V, `sysvinit` organized system states into numeric **runlevels**:
- `0`: Halt
- `1` / `S`: Single-user rescue mode
- `3`: Multi-user text mode with networking
- `5`: Multi-user graphical mode with X11
- `6`: Reboot

Services were managed by numbered shell script symlinks in `/etc/rc<runlevel>.d/` pointing to `/etc/init.d/`:
```text
/etc/rc3.d/S10network -> /etc/init.d/network
/etc/rc3.d/S20ssh     -> /etc/init.d/ssh
/etc/rc3.d/S30cron    -> /etc/init.d/cron
```
SysVinit executed these scripts sequentially in alphabetical order. Because each shell script had to fork multiple subshells (`grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `cat`), boot times were slow. Tracking processes required brittle `/var/run/*.pid` files; if a daemon double-forked and crashed, the init system had no way of knowing whether the process was alive.

## The Push for Concurrency and Containment

Modern machines feature dozens of CPU cores and hot-pluggable USB and NVMe devices. An init system cannot assume hardware is static at power-on. Modern systems require:
1. **Parallel Activation:** Booting services concurrently across available CPU cores.
2. **Reliable Process Containment:** Using Linux **cgroups** to track every child process spawned by a service, preventing orphaned daemons.
3. **Socket and Bus Activation:** Delaying daemon startup until a connection arrives on a UNIX socket or D-Bus endpoint.
